items.prompt: The Clay Corner workshop advertises a new pottery class. Its poster gives the location and fee; a digital notice shows completed pots and invites bookings. Many intended customers pass the workshop, but some have unreliable internet. No booking results are yet available. (a) Describe three advertising features in this case (6). (b) Examine how the two methods could affect customers' decisions (7). (c) Suggest a suitable communication approach (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) The poster informs through location and fee. The digital notice uses images to encourage interest. Both carry a booking invitation or information to support action. (b) Passing residents can see local details without internet. Images can help potential customers judge what the class offers, but do not establish that they will book. Customers with unreliable access may miss the digital message. Clear fee and location information can reduce uncertainty, while missing booking details could interrupt action. (c) Keep a clear local poster and use the digital notice as a complement, with consistent fee, timing and contact details. The combination fits passers-by and people who can browse remotely. Check enquiries and bookings against the intended audience before expanding spending. No current evidence proves either method produces more sales.
marking_guidance: Context: Clay Corner. Parts/allocation: (a) three message features with purpose development, 2 each = 6. (b) local information mechanism 2, visual persuasion 2, access/action limits 3 = 7. (c) combination 2, audience justification 3, evidence-based judgement 2 = 7.

items.prompt: (a) Define advertising (2). (b) Explain what is meant by an informative purpose (2). (c) Explain what is meant by a persuasive purpose (2). (d) Explain why one message can inform and persuade (2). (e) Explain why radio is a method rather than an aim (2). (f) Explain one limit of views as evidence of success (2). (g) Explain why audience location matters (2). (h) Explain one requirement for choosing a visual method (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Communication intended to inform or persuade an audience about an offer or organisation. (b) Supplying relevant details reduces uncertainty about the offer. (c) Seeking to influence preference encourages a choice. (d) A fee can inform while an image encourages preference in the same message. (e) It carries the communication rather than describing the audience effect. (f) People may see without buying, so views do not prove sales. (g) A local service needs people able to reach it; distant attention may be less useful. (h) It should show relevant appearance/details and reach people able to access the format.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a) communication + intended effect; (b) information + uncertainty; (c) preference + choice; (d) two distinct functions in one example; (e) channel + purpose contrast; (f) exposure/action distinction; (g) locality + relevance; (h) useful visual content + audience access.

objective_titles: Describe the purpose and methods of advertising

items.prompt: The Quiet Desk furniture maker wants customers to know its location and appreciate the finish of its desks. A radio announcement reaches local listeners; a printed leaflet can show photographs and dimensions. The business can afford one initial campaign. No reliable cost-per-customer or response figures are supplied. (a) Define an advertising method (2). (b) Explain two purposes relevant to the campaign (4). (c) Explain how the methods differ in meeting the stated communication needs (7). (d) Discuss which should be tried first (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Channel used to communicate advertising to an audience. (b) Inform customers of the location so they can visit. Persuade through the finish so they consider choosing the desks. (c) Radio can announce location and repeat it for local listeners, but cannot show the finish. A leaflet can display photographs and dimensions for later reference, but must reach relevant readers and images may not fully represent the object. Neither establishes actual purchase. (d) A targeted leaflet is defensible if showing finish and dimensions is central and distribution can reach potential customers. Radio may be better where listening reach is strong and finding the location is the main barrier. Given the absent response data, do not claim one has lower cost per customer. Try a method suited to the priority, monitor enquiries and consider the other if the information gap remains.
marking_guidance: Context: Quiet Desk. Parts/allocation: (a) channel 1, audience communication 1. (b) informative and persuasive purpose, each aim + case effect 2 = 4. (c) radio mechanism 2, print visual/detail mechanism 3, limits 2 = 7. (d) justified choice 2, alternative case 2, conditional judgement respecting missing evidence 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a local lunch seller should use digital advertising alone when the message is easy to update but some nearby customers lack reliable access (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: a digital message can update the menu and contact details quickly, helping connected customers find current information. Images may also encourage interest in the food. Against: local customers without access may remain unaware, and views do not prove purchases. Preparation and replies use time even without a placement fee. Judgement: combine current digital information with an accessible local message if both groups matter to the seller. The condition for digital-only communication is evidence that the relevant audience can be reached reliably and the intended information is understood. Audience fit matters more than assuming a modern channel is sufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for: current information and persuasion mechanisms, up to 4. Argument against: exclusion, uncertain action and time cost developed, up to 4. Judgement: distinct reach/access condition, 1. Total 9.
